didder.e: From Middle English didderen (“to tremble”); see dither.

d.g: In percussion, two consecutive notes played by the same hand (either RR or LL), similar to the drag, except that by convention diddles are played the same speed as the context in which they are placed.
The penis.
d.x: Paul was the first one to unzip his pants, take out his diddle, and make himself ready to pee on the wire.

d.g: Gin (the drink).
d.x: […] a long, wooden porch good for listening to coyotes and owls, with a glass of diddle at hand.

d.g: To cheat; to swindle.
d.x: 'No one ever got rich being honest,' the father said. 'Customers are there to be diddled.'

diddle.e: From dialectal duddle (“to trick”) (16th century), and diddle, duddle (“to totter”) (17th century), perhaps dissimilated from dialectal didder, dither (“to shake, tremble”), from Middle English dideren (“to shake, quiver, tremble”) and Middle English bididren (“to seduce, deceive”), from Old English bedidrian, bedyderi …

d.g: Not to have the same traits or characteristics; to be unalike or distinct.
d.x: These shoes only differ from those ones in having slightly longer laces.

d.g: To be separated in quantity.
d.x: The numbers 3 and 21 differ by 18.

d.g: To have diverging opinions, disagree.
d.x:
May 11, 1827, George Canning, Changes in the Administration
I differ from the honourable baronet on both these subjects

d.g: A program that diffs, a diff.

differ.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- Proto-Indo-European *bʰéreti Proto-Italic *ferō Latin ferō Latin differō Old French differerbor. …

d.g: To modify so as to create a difference or distinction.
d.x: A humble instance of Ablaut may be quoted which took place in the seventeenth century, when the word then was differentiated into the two forms then and than.

d.g: To show or be the difference or distinction between things.
d.x: What differentiates an alligator from a crocodile?

d.g: To recognize as different or distinct.
d.x: How do you differentiate a fake smile from a genuine one?

d.g: To calculate the derivative of a function.

differentiate.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- Proto-Indo-European *bʰéreti Proto-Italic *ferō Latin ferō Latin differō Latin differēns Proto-Indo-European *-yós Proto-Italic *-ios Old Latin -ios Latin -ius Latin -ia Latin differentia New Latin different …

d.g: To cause diffraction
To undergo diffraction

diffract.e: From Latin diffractus (“past participle of diffringo (“to shatter, to break into pieces”)”).

d.g: Alternative spelling of digitalize.

digitalise.e: English digital English -ise English digitalise From digital + -ise.

d.g: Synonym of digitize.
To administer digitalis.
Non-Oxford British English standard spelling of digitize.
d.x: Complying with its obligations of being a charitable organisation to provide educational material to all, the RCTS is digitising all its printed matter.

d.g: To represent something (such as an image or sound) as a structured sequence of binary digits.
d.x: When you digitize a visual image, you are translating it into digital signals so that it can be broken down into pixels and loaded into the computer.

d.g: To quantize a continuous or analog value; to convert it into a discrete value.

digitize.e: English digit Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íďďō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō)bor. Late Latin -izōder. Middle French -iserbor. Middle English -isen English -ize English digitize From digit + -ize.

d.g: To invest with dignity or honour.
d.x: Your worth will dignify our feast.

d.g: To give distinction to.
d.x:
Or, when more deeply moved, he would exclaim--
"As noble thoughts the inward being grace,
So noble whiskers dignify the face."

d.g: To exalt in rank.
To treat as worthy or acceptable; to indulge or condone by acknowledging.
d.x: I will not dignify that comment with a response.

dignify.e: From Old French dignifier, from Late Latin dignificare, from dignus (“worthy”) + ficare (in comp.), facere (“to make”). See deign and fact.

d.g: To step or turn aside; to deviate; to swerve; especially, to turn aside from the main subject of attention, or course of argument, in writing or speaking.
d.x: Moreover she beginneth to digress in latitude.

d.g: To turn aside from the right path; to transgress; to offend.

digress.e: From Latin digressum, past participle of digredi.

d.g: To cause to become ruined or put into disrepair.
d.x: If the bishop, parson, or vicar, etc., dilapidates the buildings, or cuts down the timber of the patrimony[…]

d.g: To squander or waste.
d.x: The patrimony of the bishopric of Oxon was much dilapidated.

dilapidate.e: From Latin dilapidō (“to scatter, consume, throw away”) + -ate (verb-forming suffix), from dis- (“asunder”) + lapidō (“to stone”), from lapis (“stone”). Compare French dilapider.

d.g: To enlarge; to make bigger.
d.x: The eye doctor put drops in my eye to dilate the pupil so he could see the nerve better.

d.g: To become wider or larger; to expand.
d.x: His heart dilates and glories in his strength.

d.g: To speak largely and copiously; to dwell in narration; to enlarge; with "on" or "upon".
d.x: Do me the favour to dilate at full / What hath befallen of them and thee till now.

d.g: To use a dilator to widen (something, such as a vagina).
d.x: He gave her some of the dilators he used to dilate her vagina shortly after the surgery and encouraged her to do it frequently.

dilate.e: First attested in 1393, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English dilaten, from Old French dilater, from Latin dīlātō (“to spread out”), from dī- + lātus (“wide”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of dilatate.

d.g: Alternative spelling of dilly-dally.
To make smaller.
To become less or smaller.
To make appear smaller than in reality; to dismiss as unimportant.
To lessen the authority or dignity of; to put down; to degrade; to abase; to weaken; to nerf (in gaming).

diminish.e: Formed under the influence of both diminue (from Old French diminuer, from Latin dīminuo) and minish.

d.g: To eat; to eat dinner or supper.
To give a dinner to; to furnish with the chief meal; to feed.

dine.e: From Middle English dynen, from Old French disner (“to dine, eat the main meal of the day”), from Vulgar Latin *disiūnāre (“to eat breakfast”), from *disieiūnāre (“to break the fast”), from Late Latin, from dis- + iēiūnō (“to fast”), from Latin ieiūnus.

d.g: Alternative spelling of diphthongize.
To change to a diphthong, as by inserting or removing a vowel.
d.x: Some of these [monophthongs] will be diphthongised under the influence of following sounds.

d.g: To become a diphthong.
To render unable; to take away an ability of, as by crippling.
To impair the physical or mental abilities of; to cause a serious, permanent injury.
d.x: Falling off the horse disabled him.

d.g: To deactivate, to make inoperational (especially of a function of an electronic or mechanical device).
d.x: The pilot had to disable the autopilot of his airplane.

disable.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. …

d.g: To free (someone) of a misconception or misapprehension; to unveil a falsehood held by (someone).
d.x: I had been too profoundly disabused of life's dearest illusions ever again to allow of their sweet engrossment.

disabuse.e: From dis- + abuse. Compare French désabuser.

d.g: The absence or reverse of accord.
Disharmony.
To fail to be in accord; to dissent.
d.x: He stated the case but I did disaccord.

disaccord.e: From Middle English disacorden, from Anglo-Norman desacorder.

d.g: To cause a loss of affection, sympathy or loyalty in; to alienate or estrange.

disaffect.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English affect English disaffect From dis- + affect.

d.g: To deforest.
To change the status of land from that of a forest to ordinary land.

disafforest.e: From Middle English disafforeten, from Anglo-Norman disaforester and its probable etymon Latin disafforestō. By surface analysis, dis- + afforest.

d.g: To fail to agree; to have a different opinion or belief.
d.x: John disagreed with Mary frequently.

d.g: To fail to conform or correspond with.
d.x: My results in the laboratory consistently disagree with yours.

disagree.e: From Middle English disagre (“to refuse to assent to”), from Anglo-Norman disagreer, disagrer, desagreer (“to refuse assent”), from Old French desagreer, desagrëer (“to be disagreeable; to be unpleasant”) (modern French désagréer (“to displease”)); the English word is analysable as dis- + agree.

d.g: To refuse to allow.
d.x: The prisoners were disallowed to contact with a lawyer.

d.g: To reject as invalid, untrue, or improper.
d.x: The goal was disallowed because the player was offside.

d.g: To overrule a colonial legislation by the sovereign-in-privy council.

disallow.e: From Middle English disallowen, desallowen, a borrowing from Anglo-Norman desalouer, Old French desalöer. By surface analysis, dis- + allow.

d.g: To remove ambiguities from; to make less ambiguous; to clarify or specify which of multiple possibilities applies – e.g., possible meanings of an ambiguous statement – or to invite or require this.
To distinguish one word or lexical unit (from a different one which has a similar form).
d.x: When necessary, the Greek spelling is disambiguated by an appended phonetic transcription.

disambiguate.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- Proto-Indo-European *h₂ent- Proto-Indo-European *-s Proto-Indo-European *h₂énts? Proto-Indo-European *h₂m̥bʰíder. …

d.g: To vanish.
To go missing; to become a missing person.
d.x: Eighteen years after Jaycee Dugard disappeared in 1991, she was found alive in the summer of 2009.

d.g: To go away; to become lost.
d.x: A turban and loincloth soaked in blood had been found; also a staff. These properties were known to have belonged to a toddy drawer. He had disappeared.

d.g: To make vanish; especially, to abduct or murder for political reasons.
d.x: The Chinese government is well-known for disappearing particularly vocal political dissidents.

disappear.e: From Middle English disapeeren, equivalent to dis- + appear. Displaced native Old English fordwīnan. Displaced native Old English cwincan, whose causative persists as quench (“put out (fire)”).

d.g: To sadden or displease (someone) by underperforming, or by not delivering something promised or hoped for.
d.x: His lack of respect disappointed her.

d.g: To deprive (someone of something expected or hoped for).
d.x: […] you shan’t be disappointed of a wedding—you shall come to mine.

d.g: To fail to meet (an expectation); to fail to fulfil (a hope).
d.x: “But perhaps your accommodations—your cottage—your furniture—have disappointed your expectations?”

d.g: To show (an opinion, belief, etc.) to be mistaken.
d.x: I am sure you will not disappoint my opinion of you, by failing at any time to treat your aunt Norris with the respect and attention that are due to her.

disappoint.e: From Middle French desapointer (compare French désappointer). The word originally meant to "dispossess of appointed office", and eventually broadened to mean "to frustrate the expectations or desires of" and "defeat the realization or fulfillment of".

d.g: To condemn; to consider wrong or inappropriate; used with of.
d.x: She disapproves of rap music because of its sometimes aggressive lyrics.

d.g: To have or express an unfavorable opinion.
d.x: Green washing schemes of corporations are disapproved by Greenpeace activists.

d.g: To refuse to approve; reject.

disapprove.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. …

d.g: To deprive of weapons; to deprive of the means of attack or defense; to render defenseless.
To deprive of the means or the disposition to harm; to render harmless or innocuous.
d.x: to disarm a man's wrath

d.g: To lay down arms; to stand down.
To reduce one's own military forces.

disarm.e: From Middle English desarmen (“to divest of arms”), from Anglo-Norman desarmer.

d.g: To undo the arrangement of; to disorder; to derange.
d.x: Stay, dear, you will disarrange your curls—let me untie your hat.

disarrange.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd Proto-Italic *ad Proto-Italic *ad- Latin ad- Old French a- Proto-Indo-European *(H)rek-der. …

d.g: To disjoint.
To amputate (a limb) at a joint without cutting the bone.

disarticulate.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English articulate English disarticulate From dis- + articulate.

d.g: To take to pieces; to reverse the process of assembly.
d.x: To perform the repair it was necessary to disassemble most of the mechanism.

d.g: To convert machine code to a human-readable, mnemonic form.

disassemble.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. …

d.g: To separate (oneself); to dissolve one's association with a person, group, or situation.
d.x: After the scandal, the political party disassociated itself from the questionable candidate.

d.g: To separate into smaller discrete units, as with analysis.
d.x: The problem is easier to understand if you disassociate the variables.

d.g: To separate; to disunite; to disintegrate; to dissolve.
d.x: The fibers of this nonwoven textile disassociated when I tried to wash it.

d.g: Alternative form of dissociate.

disassociate.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English associate English disassociate From dis- + associate.

d.g: To strongly and solemnly refuse to own or acknowledge; to deny responsibility for, approbation of, and the like.
d.x: He was charged with embezzlement, but he disavows the crime.

d.g: To deny; to show the contrary of; to deny legitimacy or achievement of any kind.
d.x: Because of her dissatisfaction, she now disavows the merits of socialism.

disavow.e: From dis- + avow, or from Old French desavouer.

d.g: To break up or (cause to) cease to exist; to disperse.
d.x: The president wanted to disband the scandal-plagued agency.

disband.e: Attested since the 1590s, from Middle French desbander (Modern French débander), from des- (English dis-) + bande (English band), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ- (“to tie”). By surface analysis, dis- + band.

d.g: To expel from the bar, or the legal profession; to deprive (an attorney, barrister, or counselor) of his or her status and privileges as such.
To exclude (a person) from something.
d.x: The friends of Holmes have been criticising the action of the board in disbarring him on the ground that it was too severe […]

disbar.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English bar English disbar From dis- + bar.

d.g: To not believe; to exercise disbelief.
d.x: If you disbelieve such people, then keep disbelieving them for as long as you live or want.

d.g: To actively deny (a statement, opinion or perception).
d.x: He chose to disbelieve the bad news as inconceivable.

d.g: To cease to believe.
d.x: He never "revolted" against Christianity; only, reluctantly and gradually, disbelieved it.

disbelieve.e: Coined circa 1640, from dis- + believe. Compare misbelieve.

d.g: To remove buds from a plant in order to promote growth and health in the remaining buds.
To remove horn-buds from a young calf, lamb or goat kid, to prevent growth of horns.

disbud.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English bud English disbud From dis- + bud.

d.g: To rid of a burden; to free from a load carried; to unload.
d.x: to disburden a pack animal

d.g: To free from a source of mental trouble.
d.x: My meditations […] will, I hope, be more […] calm, being thus disburdened.

disburden.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English burden English disburden From dis- + burden.

d.g: To pay out, expend; usually from a public fund or treasury.

disburse.e: From Old French desbourser (Modern French débourser). By surface analysis, dis- + burse (“purse”).

d.g: get undressed

discase.e: Latin dis- Old French des-bor. Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English case English discase From dis- + case.

d.g: To detect with the senses, especially with the eyes.
To perceive, recognize, or comprehend with the mind; to descry.
To distinguish something as being different from something else; to differentiate or discriminate.
d.x: He was too young to discern right from wrong.

d.g: To perceive differences.

discern.e: From Middle English discernen, from Old French discerner, from Latin discernere (“to separate, divide, distinguish, discern”), from dis- (“apart”) + cernere (“to distinguish”); see certain.

d.g: To tear into pieces; to rend.
To separate; to disunite.
d.x: […] to reascend the place from whence they came, and rejoin that Substance from whence they were discerped […]

discerp.e: From Latin discerpō, from dis- + carpō (“to pluck”).

d.g: To completely renounce claims to; to deny ownership of or responsibility for
d.x: He calls the Gods to witness their offence, / Disclaims the War, asserts his Innocence.

d.g: To deny (e.g. claim); to refuse.
d.x: The payment was irregularly made, if not disclaimed.

d.g: (law) To relinquish or deny having a claim; to disavow another's claim; to decline accepting, as an estate, interest, or office.
To make a caveat or admission.
d.x: I disclaim that there will be a lot of inside humor. If you don't read a.r.s often, or are a newbie, you won't get some of the gags.

disclaim.e: From Middle English disclaimen, from Anglo-Norman disclaimer, from Old French desclamer (French déclamer), des- + clamer.

d.g: To uncover; physically expose to view.
d.x: The shells being broken, […] the stone included in them is thereby disclosed and set at liberty.

d.g: To expose to the knowledge of others; to make known; state openly; reveal (something).
d.x: Her lively looks a sprightly mind disclose.

disclose.e: From Middle English disclosen, from Middle French desclos, from Old French desclore, itself from Vulgar Latin disclaudere, from Latin dis- + claudere (“to close, shut”) or as a variant of discludo, discludere (cf. disclude). By surface analysis, dis- + close.

d.g: To change or lose color.
d.x: Washing light laundry with dark may cause your clothes to discolor.

discolor.e: From Middle English discoloren, discoloren, from Old French descolorer, discolorer, equivalent to dis- + color.

d.g: remove color from
remove color from
British and Canadian standard spelling of discolor.

discolour.e: From Middle English discolouren, discoloren, from Old French discolorer, descolorer, equivalent to dis- + colour.

d.g: remove color from
To throw into a state of confusion; to befuddle or perplex.
d.x: The notes zigzag in his pieces and discombobulate the ear, just as in 12-tone works.

discombobulate.e: 1834 US, fanciful variant of discompose, discomfit, etc., originally discombobricate. The -bob- interfix may come from bobbery, meaning “commotion, noise”.

d.g: To embarrass (someone) greatly; to confuse; to perplex; to disconcert.
d.x: Don't worry. Your joke did not really discomfit me.

d.g: To defeat the plans or hopes of; to frustrate; disconcert.
d.x: In these disguises, Maitland argued, he would certainly avoid recognition, and so discomfit any mischief planned by the enemies of Margaret.

discomfit.e: From Middle English discomfiten, from Old French desconfit, past participle of desconfire (“to undo, to destroy”), from des- (“completely”), from Latin dis- + Old French confire (“to make”), from Latin cōnficiō (“to finish up, to destroy”), from com- (“with, together”) + faciō (“to do, to make”). …

d.g: To cause inconvenience to (someone).
To destroy the composure of; to disturb or agitate.
d.x: I am glad I have done being in love with him. I should not like a man who is so soon discomposed by a hot morning.

d.g: To disarrange, or throw into a state of disorder.
d.x:
If e'er with airy horns I planted heads,
Or rumpled petticoats, or tumbled beds,
Or caus'd suspicion when no soul was rude,

discompose.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English compose English discompose From dis- + compose.

d.g: To upset the composure of; to startle.
d.x: The embrace disconcerted the daughter-in-law somewhat, as the caresses of old gentlemen unshorn and perfumed with tobacco might well do.

d.g: To bring into confusion.
To frustrate, discomfit.
d.x: The emperor disconcerted the plans of his enemy.

d.g: A state of disunion.

disconcert.e: From Middle French desconcerter, from des- (“dis-”) + concerter (“to bring into agreement, organize”).

d.g: To interrupt the continuance of; to put an end to, especially as regards commercial productions; to stop producing, making, or supplying.
d.x: They plan to discontinue that design.

d.g: To consciously cease the ingestion or administration of (a pharmaceutical drug).

discontinue.e: From Old French descontinuer, equivalent to dis- + continue.

d.g: To have an unfavorable opinion of; to deprecate or disapprove of.
d.x: A town meeting was convened to discountenance riot.

d.g: To abash, embarrass or disconcert.
d.x: The hermit was somewhat discountenanced by this observation.

d.g: To refuse countenance or support to; to discourage.
d.x: These were rejected by Parliament, which discountenanced the amalgamation of competing lines but gave broad approval in theory to end-on amalgamations.

d.g: Cold treatment; disapprobation.

discountenance.e: From Middle French descontenancer (compare French décontenancer).

d.g: To extinguish the courage of; to dishearten; to depress the spirits of; to deprive of confidence; to deject.
d.x: Don't be discouraged by the amount of work left to do: you'll finish it in good time.

d.g: To persuade somebody not to do (something).
d.x: Discourage litigation. Persuade your neighbors to compromise whenever you can.

d.g: Lack of courage

discourage.e: From Middle French descourager (modern French décourager), from Old French descouragier, from des- and corage. By surface analysis, dis- + courage.

d.g: To find or learn something for the first time.
d.x: Turning the corner, I discovered a lovely little shop. I discovered that they sold widgets.

d.g: To create by moving a piece out of another piece's line of attack.
d.x: This move discovers an attack on a vital pawn.

d.g: To question (a person) as part of discovery in a lawsuit.

discover.e: From Middle English discoveren, from Old French descovrir, from Late Latin discoperīre < discooperiō, discooperīre, from Latin dis- + cooperiō. Displaced native Old English onfindan.

d.g: To converse or debate concerning a particular topic.
d.x: Let's sit down and discuss whether we should have a baby.

d.g: To examine or search thoroughly; to exhaust a remedy against, as against a principal debtor before proceeding against the surety.

discuss.e: From Middle English discussen, from Middle French and Anglo-Norman discusser (French discuter), from Latin discussus, past participle of discutiō (“to strike or shake apart, break up, scatter; examine, discuss”), from dis- (“apart”) + quatiō (“to shake”).

d.g: To remove from on board a vessel; to put on shore
d.x: The general disembarked the troops.

d.g: To go ashore out of a ship or boat; to leave a train or aircraft.
To go ashore from (a boat); to leave (a train or aircraft)
d.x: We disembarked the ferry.

disembark.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English em- English bark English embark English disembark From dis- + embark.

d.g: To get (someone) out of a difficult or embarrassing situation; to free (someone) from the embarrassment (of a situation); (often reflexive) to relieve (someone of a burden, item of clothing, etc.).
d.x: He had now disembarrassed himself of his riding-dress, and walking up to his daughter, he undid the fastening of her mask.

disembarrass.e: From dis- + embarrass. Possibly a calque of French désembarrasser. First attested in 1726 (sense 1).

d.g: To cause someone's soul, spirit, consciousness, voice, etc, to become separated from the physical body.
To separate (a part of the body) from the body.
d.x: Jerusha turned, a flush on her cheeks that wasn't makeup, a swath of steam from the vaporizer swirling around her chest, disembodying her head.

d.g: To discharge from military service or array.

disembody.e: Latin dis- Old French des-bor. Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English embody English disembody From dis- + embody.

d.g: To take or let out the bowels or interior parts of; to eviscerate.
To take or draw from the body, as the web of a spider.

disembowel.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- English embowel English disembowel From dis- + embowel.

d.g: To free or extricate from confusion
To disable (render unable)
d.x: The sight of it might damp me and disenable me to speak.

d.g: To free from illusion, false belief or enchantment; to undeceive or disillusion.
To disappoint.
To break from a mental captivation such as reverie (daydream) or preoccupation.
To remove a spell or magic enchantment from.

Wou’d almoſt tempt us to renounce his Precepts.

distract.e: Borrowed from Latin distractus, from distrahō (“to pull apart”), from dis- + trahō (“to pull”).

d.g: To seize somebody's property in place of, or to force, payment of a debt.

distrain.e: From Middle English distreynen, from Old French destraindre, from Latin distringō (“to pull asunder”), from dis- (“apart”) + stringō (“to draw tight, strain”).

d.g: To divide into portions and dispense.
d.x: He distributed the bread amongst his followers.

d.g: To supply to retail outlets.
d.x: The agency distributes newspapers to local shops.

d.g: To deliver or pass out.
d.x: A network of children distributes flyers to every house.

d.g: To scatter or spread.
d.x: I raked the soil then distributed grass seed.

distribute.e: PIE word *tréyes From Latin distributus, past participle of distribuere (“to divide, distribute”), from dis- (“apart”) + tribuere (“to give, impart”); see tribute.

d.g: to confuse a quiet, constant state or a calm, continuous flow, in particular: thoughts, actions or liquids.
d.x: The noisy ventilation disturbed me during the exam.

d.g: to divert, redirect, or alter by disturbing.
d.x: A mudslide disturbed the course of the river.

d.g: to have a negative emotional impact; to cause emotional distress or confusion.

disturb.e: From Middle English destourben, from Anglo-Norman distourber and Old French destorber, from Latin disturbare, intensifying for turbare (“to throw into disorder”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)twerH-, *(s)turH- (“to rotate, swirl, twirl, move around”).

d.g: To cause to cease to be unified; to split up or dissociate.
To cause disagreement or alienation among or within.
d.x: If they cannot disunite them by domestic broils, then they engage their neighbours against them.

d.g: To separate, sever, or split.
d.x: I have discovered how to disunite that force and that particle.

d.g: To disintegrate; to come apart.
d.x:
You cannot bind me more to you, my lord.
Farewell till we renew... I trust, renew
A converse ne'er to disunite again.

disunite.e: Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *d(w)is- Proto-Italic *dis- Latin dis- Old French des-bor. ▲ Latin dis-bor. Middle English dis- English dis- Proto-Indo-European *ís? Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos Proto-Italic *oinos Old Latin oinos Latin ūnus Proto-Indo-European *-yétider. …

d.g: To wander about.
To stray from a subject or theme.
d.x: The fallen guillotine blade is replaced with a call to awareness that, as we have seen, divagates from Szpiner's "Ayez pitié des enfants."

divagate.e: First attested in 1599; borrowed from Latin dīvagātus, perfect active participle of dīvagor (“to wander here and there”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from Latin dis- (“in different direction”) + vagor (“to wander”). Cognate with French divaguer.

d.g: To spread apart; to (cause to) diverge or branch off.
Having wide angles between the branches.

divaricate.e: The verb is first attested in 1623, the adjective in 1788; borrowed from Latin dīvāricātus, perfect passive participle of dīvāricō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from dis- + vāricō (“to straddle, to stretch (the legs) apart”), from vāricus (“straddling”).

d.g: To run apart; to separate; to tend into different directions.
d.x: Two roads diverged in a yellow wood, / And sorry I could not travel both / […]

d.g: To become different; to run apart; to separate; to tend into different directions.
d.x: Both stories start out the same way, but they diverge halfway through.

d.g: To separate, to tend into a different direction (from another line or path).
d.x: The sidewalk runs next to the street for a few miles, then diverges from it and turns north.

d.g: To become different, to separate (from another line or path).
d.x: The software is pretty good, except for a few cases where its behavior diverges from user expectations.

diverge.e: From Medieval Latin dīvergō (“bend away from, go in a different direction”), from Latin dī- + vergō (“bend”).

d.g: To make (something) diverse or varied in form or quality; to give variety to (something) to distinguish by numerous aspects or differences.
To make the scope of (business, investments, etc.) diverse, especially so as to balance and mitigate risks.

diversify.e: Borrowed from Middle French diversifier, equivalent to diverse + -ify.

d.g: To turn aside from a course.
d.x: The workers diverted the stream away from the road.

d.g: To distract.
d.x: Don't let him divert your attention; keep your eye on the ball.

d.g: To entertain or amuse (by diverting the attention)
d.x: We are amused by a tale, diverted by a comedy.

divert.e: From Middle English diverten, Old French divertir (“to turn or go different ways, part, separate, divert”), from Latin di- (“apart”) + vertere (“to turn”); see verse.

d.g: To strip, deprive, or dispossess (someone) of something (such as a right, passion, privilege, or prejudice).
d.x: You shall never divest me of my right to free speech.

d.g: To sell off or be rid of through sale, especially of a subsidiary.
d.x: In 2011, the company divested an 81% majority stake in its foreign subsidiary.

divest.e: Alteration of devest, from Middle French devester (“strip of possessions”), from Old French desvestir, from des- (“dis-”) + vestir (“to clothe”).

d.g: To make public or known; to communicate to the public; to tell (information, especially a secret) so that it may become generally known.
d.x: I will never divulge that secret to anyone.

d.g: To indicate publicly; to proclaim.
d.x: God... marks The just man, and divulges him through heaven.

divulge.e: Inherited from Middle English divulgen, from Latin dīvulgō + -en (verb-forming suffix), from dī- (“widely”) + vulgō (“to make known, announce; to publish”).

d.g: To dress with flax for spinning.
To dress with clothes; attire; deck; bedizen.
d.x: Like a tragedy queen he has dizen'd her out, / Or rather like tragedy giving a rout.

d.g: To dress showily; adorn; dress out.

dizen.e: From dialectal dize (“to put tow on a distaff”), from Middle English *disen, from Old English *disan, *disian, from *dise, *disen (“bunch of flax on a distaff”), from Proto-Germanic *disanō (“distaff”), of unknown origin, equivalent to dize + -en. …
